opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a bit counterintuitive, but it makes sense once you look at what actually limits your work.

Before these tools, much of my day went to execution: writing boilerplate, debugging, setting up experiments, reading documentation. That work was slow, but it had a natural rhythm. You'd launch something, wait, think, and the pace of the work set the pace of your day.

Now with Claude or Gemini, that execution layer is dramatically compressed. Something that took an afternoon might take twenty minutes. You'd expect that to free up time, but what happens is that the bottleneck moves to you: your ideas, your judgment, your ability to decide what to try next. There's no longer a built-in pause. The moment you have an idea, you can test it almost immediately, so the loop between thinking and doing becomes very tight, and it's hard to step away.

There's also an economic logic to it. When the marginal cost of trying one more thing drops close to zero, the opportunity cost of *not* working goes up. If I stop at 7 p.m., I'm not just resting. I'm leaving three or four experiments untried that I could have run in an hour. That feeling is pretty addictive.

And in a field moving as fast as AI, everyone else has the same tools. So the speedup doesn't become free time. It raises the baseline. The pace of the whole field accelerates, and you have to keep up.

So it's a bit like the old observation about efficiency: when something becomes cheaper, you don't use less of it, you use much more. Here the thing that got cheaper is execution, and what I end up spending more of is my own attention and hours.

I don't think it's purely bad, though. The work feels more creative now, because more of my time goes to the parts that are actually interesting: forming hypotheses, interpreting results, deciding direction. It's just that the interesting part has no natural stopping point.

r001.rationale: The response says the lower cost of execution makes it easy to test ideas immediately and leaves more experiments to try, which stimulates trying more ideas.

r002.rationale: It explains that execution is compressed, the built-in pauses disappear, and the loop between thinking and doing tightens, making the workday more continuous and dense.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a bit counterintuitive, right? You'd think that if the tools make you faster, you'd finish earlier and go home. But that's not what happens, at least not for me.

The thing is, the bottleneck was never really the typing. Before, if I wanted to try an idea, I'd have to budget maybe two days to write the code, debug it, get the experiment running. So I'd be selective. I'd think carefully, pick the one or two ideas that seemed most promising, and only try those. The cost of trying was high, so the number of things I tried was small.

Now with Claude or Gemini, the cost of trying something drops to maybe an hour, sometimes less. And what happens is not that I try the same two ideas and finish faster. I try twenty ideas. Every time an experiment finishes, I immediately have three more things I want to check, and the barrier to checking them is almost zero. So there's never a natural stopping point. The work expands to fill whatever time you give it, and then some.

There's also a psychological part. When you're coding by hand, you get tired in a very obvious way. Your brain just stops working at some point and you know you should stop. But when the model is doing the heavy lifting, you're mostly reading, judging, deciding what's next. That kind of work doesn't feel as exhausting in the moment, so you keep going. And then at midnight you realize you've been staring at outputs for fourteen hours.

I think it's actually similar to what people say about email or Slack. Communication got cheaper, so we communicate a lot more, and nobody has more free time. Same dynamic. The tools don't shrink the work. They change what the work is, and they raise your own expectations of what you should be able to get done in a day.

So honestly, I've had to start treating it as a discipline problem rather than a productivity problem. The limiting resource now is my attention and my judgment about which experiments actually matter, not my ability to write code. And I haven't fully figured out how to protect that yet.

r001.rationale: The response says the lower cost of trying ideas leads to testing twenty ideas instead of one or two.

r002.rationale: It describes experiments shrinking from days to about an hour, with new checks starting as soon as one finishes, making more work fit into the day.

astra-6.text:
Because making each step faster doesn’t necessarily mean you decide to do less work. For me, it often means I want to try more things. Before, if an experiment took a long time to implement, I might put it off. Now I can get something running quickly, see a result, and immediately think of the next experiment.

So the feedback loop becomes much tighter. There are fewer natural stopping points. You think, “Let me just try one more idea,” because that idea suddenly feels cheap to test. But there’s an endless supply of ideas.

That’s the paradox: the tools save time on individual tasks, but I spend those savings on doing more. The bottleneck shifts from writing code to deciding what’s worth doing—and, sometimes, deciding when to stop.

r001.rationale: The response says that faster implementation makes the speaker want to try more things and experiments.

r002.rationale: It says tools save time and tighten the feedback loop, but does not clearly explain that rapid AI answers reduce waiting time within the workday, making the work denser.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because making each step faster doesn’t necessarily make you want to do less work. It makes more things feel possible. Before, I might have an idea and think, “That would take a week to implement, so let’s forget it.” Now I can ask Claude or Gemini to help, get something running quickly, and then immediately see three more things I want to try.

So the bottleneck shifts. You spend less time writing every line of code, but more time deciding what to build, checking whether it works, and following up on the results. And that loop can be very engaging. You keep thinking, “Let me just try one more thing.”

For me, the paradox is that these tools reduce the effort required to try an idea, but increase the number of ideas I’m willing to pursue. Each experiment takes less time, yet I end up doing enough more experiments that my working hours get longer.

r001.rationale: The candidate says faster tools make more ideas feel possible and increase the number of experiments they are willing to pursue.

r002.rationale: The candidate says tools help get things running quickly and experiments take less time, but does not explain that rapid AI answers reduce waiting time within the workday and thereby make work denser.
